findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Capital Programme - Appendix 1 & 2
findings.headline: £17.9m of capital budgets from 2025-26 did not progress and have been rolled into 2026-27
findings.detail: The Capital Plan Outturn Report for 2025-26 identified £17.9m of capital budgets that were not spent in the previous year. These have been added to the 2026-27 programme amendments, requiring the council to deliver both a £42.6m base capital programme and the carried-forward slippage within a single year.
findings.matters: A lender would need to assess whether the council has sufficient delivery capacity and resources to execute an enlarged capital programme without further slippage. Sustained capital delays can indicate resource constraints, project management weaknesses, or planning approval delays that affect execution capability.
findings.figures: £17,888,500 slippage; total 2026-27 capital budget £42,582,200
findings.quote: Capital Plan Outturn Report 2025-26 - Slippage of capital budgets from 2025/26 17,888,500

findings.paper_title: General Fund and HRA Reserves
findings.headline: Officers and Scrutiny Committee hold opposing views on whether to spend down reserves before unitarisation
findings.detail: The Scrutiny Committee believes reserves should be deployed on Charnwood-based projects by March 2027 before transition to the unitary. Officers acknowledge this is 'valid' but argue that spending reserves now reduces resources available to the new unitary council, and that the new council needs sufficient reserves to operate 'without further external borrowing in order to facilitate the future financial sustainability of this council'.
findings.matters: This unresolved policy disagreement affects the financial position the new unitary authority will inherit and signals governance tension over reserve management during a critical transition
findings.figures: No quantified impact; affects deployment of £10.4m GF and £11.9m HRA reserves
findings.quote: The view that funds should be spent in Charnwood prior to LGR is valid. However, funds spent now reduce the financial resources available to the new unitary council and it is equally valid to form a view that the new council should commence operations with sufficient reserves to retain the minimum set by the Section 151 officer, and to enable continued function of operations without further external borrowing

findings.paper_title: General Fund and HRA Reserves
findings.headline: Structural Changes Order from March 2027 creates a narrow window to deploy reserves before local government reorganisation takes effect
findings.detail: Officers confirm that the Structural Changes Order and Section 24 notice restricting council expenditure and asset management are 'extremely likely' to come into force from March 2027. This creates 'limited time' to expend reserves on capital schemes or revenue spending that would breach the restrictions once they take effect.
findings.matters: The impending restriction order creates both time pressure to deploy reserves and regulatory risk if spending decisions are made incorrectly; the new unitary council will inherit the consequences of deployment decisions made now
findings.figures: March 2027 restriction date
findings.quote: Whilst precise dates are not yet known, it is extremely likely the Structural Changes Order (SCO) and associated Section 24 notice restricting Council expenditure and asset management activities will come into force from March 2027, giving limited time to expend funds on capital schemes or revenue expenditure that would fall foul of the SCO rules.

findings.paper_title: General Fund and HRA Reserves
findings.headline: HRA reserves are trending towards the minimum level set by the s151 officer
findings.detail: While General Fund reserves sit 'comfortably above the minimum level set by the Section 151 officer', HRA reserves are actively declining toward minimum thresholds. Officers note this situation is 'being closely monitored', signalling awareness of tightening headroom in the housing account.
findings.matters: An HRA with reserves at minimum level has no capacity to absorb pressures (void periods, repair spikes, welfare costs) without breaching prudential borrowing rules or cutting services
findings.figures: HRA reserves trending to s151 officer minimum; no absolute figures given
findings.quote: HRA reserves are trending towards the minimum level set out by the s151 officer. As point (ii) above notes, this situation is being closely monitored.

findings.paper_title: General Fund and HRA Reserves
findings.headline: HRA and General Fund capital plans exceed available reserves by £17.3m and £10.1m respectively, forcing borrowing
findings.detail: The HRA capital plan of £29.2m exceeds available reserves of £11.9m. The General Fund capital plan of £20.5m exceeds available reserves of £10.4m. Officers confirm that 'virtually all of future HRA capital expenditure will need to be financed through borrowing' and that even using all available General Fund reserves above minimum working balance will likely require General Fund borrowing as well.
findings.matters: A council forced to borrow for routine capital spending rather than use reserves faces higher future revenue pressure through interest and MRP charges, particularly concerning during a major reorganisation when the new unitary will need to establish financial stability
findings.figures: General Fund capital plan £20.5m vs reserves £10.4m (shortfall £10.1m); HRA capital plan £29.2m vs reserves £11.9m (shortfall £17.3m)
findings.quote: Virtually all of future HRA capital expenditure will need to be financed through borrowing, whilst even if all available General Fund reserves above the minimum working balance were used, it is still likely that it would be necessary to finance some of the General Fund capital plan via borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Planning delays are causing capital slippage and creating timing risk on government-mandated Right to Buy receipt deadlines
findings.detail: The council's plan to purchase 10 affordable housing units in 2025/26 was delayed due to unresolved planning matters affecting the wider site, with properties eventually purchased in April 2026, four months late. This demonstrates that the council faces planning-driven execution risks that could cause it to miss government deadlines on Right to Buy receipt spending.
findings.matters: Planning delays are creating material financial risk through potential clawback of receipts and highlight governance and execution challenges in capital delivery
findings.figures: 10 properties planned for 2025/26; purchased April 2026
findings.quote: however due to a delay in resolving planning matters, for the wider site, the properties were eventually purchased in April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Food waste vehicle scheme is fully slipping with warning that additional budget may be required
findings.detail: The £1.463m budget for household food waste caddies and collection vehicles is being fully carried forward into 2026/27 due to delayed delivery. The report explicitly warns that additional budget may be required for the vehicles, meaning the eventual cost could exceed the current provision.
findings.matters: Full budget slippage plus a warning that additional spend may be needed indicates cost control and specification management issues
findings.figures: £1.463m budget requested as slippage
findings.quote: Additional budget may be required for additional required specification to the vehicles.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Enterprise Zone budget of £5.8m remains unspent since 2023 with only autumn review planned
findings.detail: A £5.8m budget for the Enterprise Zone was created in 2023. Part of it (£4.2m) was advanced to Charnwood Campus in October 2023 and is being reclaimed over 15 years. The remaining £5.8m has never been deployed and is being carried forward again into 2026/27 with only a vague commitment to review the approach in autumn.
findings.matters: A major capital sum sitting undeployed for three years suggests the council has not developed a credible capital deployment plan and raises questions about capital planning capability
findings.figures: £5.8m undeployed budget, original £10m created, £4.2m paid to Charnwood Campus October 2023
findings.quote: The remaining budget of £5.8m has been carried forward since this time and further carry forward into 2026/27 is assumed for the purposes of this report; however, this approach will be reviewed in the autumn.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Right to Buy receipt clawback risk if council misses government spending deadlines
findings.detail: The council has agreed with government to use Right to Buy receipts to purchase affordable housing. Spending deadlines must be met or the receipts must be returned with interest. The planned purchase of 10 properties in 2025/26 slipped to April 2026 due to planning delays, demonstrating that the council is at risk of missing these government-imposed deadlines.
findings.matters: This creates a specific financial liability that could impact the council's accounts if deadlines are missed and receipts must be returned with interest
findings.figures: £1.156m slippage on £1.210m budget
findings.quote: If the budget is not spent, the Council would need to return the receipts to the Government, with interest.

findings.paper_title: Capital Monitoring - Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: General Fund capital delivered at only 25% despite £22m budget
findings.detail: The council spent £5.5m of £22m General Fund capital budget in 2025/26. Live schemes spent 37%, block sums 35%, and provisional schemes 0%. This very low overall delivery rate requires £16m to be carried forward into 2026/27, representing a substantial backlog and delivery execution risk.
findings.matters: Poor capital deployment suggests the council struggles to execute its capital programme, which creates risk that future capital schemes may also slip
findings.quote: Capital expenditure on General Fund projects was £5.5m being 25% of the budget

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Position (General Fund and HRA) Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Agency staffing costs of £2,089k General Fund and £963k HRA driven by recruitment difficulties attributed to Local Government Reorganisation impact
findings.detail: Both funds are heavily dependent on agency staff due to persistent recruitment challenges. General Fund agency costs reached £2,089k (offset by £1,991k salary savings from vacancies, resulting in net £51k adverse). HRA agency costs of £963k reflect the same issue across repairs and maintenance roles. The council attributes this to Local Government Reorganisation disruption and has approved a pay policy review for 2026/27 to address it.
findings.matters: Structural recruitment difficulties indicate either external labour market pressure or internal workplace issues; heavy reliance on expensive agency staff constrains budget flexibility and suggests operational capacity is stretched
findings.figures: £2,089k General Fund agency costs, £963k HRA agency costs, £2,385k planning-related agency spend
findings.quote: Certain service areas are experiencing ongoing issues around recruitment to vacant posts and is difficult to resolve. The impact of Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) cannot be underestimated as this can impact on the recruitment process.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Position (General Fund and HRA) Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Void loss £614k adverse; dwelling rent income 4% below budget despite net reduction of 113 void units
findings.detail: HRA void loss overspent by £614k and dwelling rent income fell £95k short of budget (4% variance). While the council reduced net void numbers by 113 units during the year (621 voids repaired vs 505 prior year), the remaining voids and costs associated with sheltered accommodation marked for disposal continue to depress income.
findings.matters: Void losses directly reduce HRA rental income and the council has not yet stabilised this cost; with only £18k reserve buffer, further void deterioration would breach minimum reserves
findings.figures: £614k void loss overspend, £95k rent income shortfall (4% of budget), 113 net reduction in voids, 621 void repairs vs 505 prior year
findings.quote: The 2025/26 rent income for dwellings was £95k lower than the budget which equates to a 4% variance. Void loss is still above budget with a £614k overspend.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Position (General Fund and HRA) Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Re-let repairs overspend £1,780k to clear void backlog; new regulatory compliance costs (Awaab's Law) driving baseline repair inflation
findings.detail: HRA repairs and maintenance overspent by £1,886k total. Re-let repairs alone were £1,780k adverse due to void backlog clearance. Beyond backlog work, the council faces new non-discretionary compliance costs: £219k for enhanced legionella mitigation, £617k in general repairs including damp and mould remediation under Awaab's Law (effective October 2025), and £504k for technical support on major works.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance costs from Awaab's Law and legionella standards are permanent additions to baseline operating costs; they cannot be deferred and signal rising structural costs in social housing management
findings.figures: £1,886k total repairs overspend, £1,780k re-let repairs, £219k legionella, £617k general repairs, £504k technical support
findings.quote: General Repairs for 2025/26 is a £617k overspend due to increased activity and pricing in materials and services. These costs include damp and mould remedial and prevention works undertaken in response to new legislation, Awaab's Law which came in to effect in October 2025.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Position (General Fund and HRA) Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Financing Fund depleted; council explicitly warns 'financing costs are likely to increase in future years'
findings.detail: The HRA Housing Financing Fund balance fell to £3,212k. The outturn report explicitly cautions that the depletion of this fund alongside capital receipt drawdowns will lead to increased financing costs ahead. This year's £2.0m PWLB debt repayment was funded through internal borrowing rather than external refinancing.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion combined with a shift to internal borrowing for debt repayment signals that the council's financing flexibility is tightening; an explicit forecast of rising financing costs indicates structural pressure
findings.figures: Housing Financing Fund £3,212k, £76m PWLB debt outstanding, £2.0m annual repayment, internal borrowing used instead of PWLB
findings.quote: However, the depletion of the HRA Financing Fund, alongside the use of Capital Receipts, shown in the table above, suggests that financing costs are likely to increase in future years.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Position (General Fund and HRA) Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: Right to buy sales of 57 units nearly three times the 22 budgeted, accelerating asset depletion
findings.detail: Right to buy completions in 2025/26 reached 57 sales against a budget of 22, representing 2.6x the expected level. This significantly exceeds projections and will erode the HRA's housing stock and future rental income base.
findings.matters: Accelerated asset depletion through right to buy reduces both the council's long-term rental income capacity and the asset base available to support borrowing; the rapid pace suggests limited forecasting accuracy
findings.figures: 57 actual sales vs 22 budgeted
findings.quote: Right to buy sales were budgeted at 22 sales, compared with 57 actual sales.

findings.paper_title: Revenue Monitoring Position (General Fund and HRA) Outturn 2025/26
findings.headline: HRA core reserve of £1,608k is only £18k above the minimum required, following a £3,004k deficit outturn
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account posted a £3,004k deficit for 2025/26, primarily from £1,886k overspend on repairs and maintenance and £614k void loss. The core reserve closing balance of £1,608k sits only marginally above the Section 151 officer's minimum of £1,590k, leaving minimal buffer for future pressures.
findings.matters: A reserve only £18k above minimum indicates the council has very little capacity to absorb further adverse variances or unexpected costs in the HRA; any deterioration in void or repair costs would breach the minimum reserve requirement
findings.figures: £3,004k deficit, £1,608k reserve (£18k above minimum), £1,886k repairs overspend, £614k void loss
findings.quote: At the 31 March 2026 the core HRA reserve stood at £1,608k. This balance is slightly above (£18k) the minimum balance set out by the Section 151 officer

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for 2025/26 Internal Audit Annual Report
findings.headline: External quality assessment of the internal audit function has been deferred beyond the standard five-year cycle.
findings.detail: The last external quality assessment of the internal audit function was completed in December 2020. The next assessment was scheduled for 2026/27 but has been deferred. Global Internal Audit Standards require independent external assessment at least every 5 years; this council has not had such validation in over 5.5 years.
findings.matters: External validation of the internal audit function is a key governance control that provides independent assurance the audit function itself is operating effectively. A deferred external assessment undermines confidence in audit findings.
findings.figures: External assessment last completed December 2020; due for 5-year cycle review but deferred to 2026/27
findings.quote: An external quality assessment was last completed in December 2020, with no significant issues identified. A further external assessment has been deferred and will take place during 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for 2025/26 Internal Audit Annual Report
findings.headline: Markets audit identified that appropriate insurance is not in place, along with incomplete reconciliations and missing risk assessments.
findings.detail: The Markets audit (Limited Assurance) found multiple control failures: appropriate insurance not being in place, reconciliations not fully completed, risk assessments not completed and authorised, training gaps, and policy misalignment. This represents unhedged financial and operational risk on a council service.
findings.matters: Missing insurance on council operations is a material unhedged risk exposure. Combined with incomplete reconciliations and missing risk assessments, this indicates financial controls over the markets operation are inadequate.
findings.figures: Markets audit received Limited Assurance with 1 high and 6 medium priority recommendations
findings.quote: Weaknesses were identified in related to appropriate insurance not being in place, reconciliations not being fully completed, risk assessments not being completed and authorised, training requirements, policy alignment.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for 2025/26 Internal Audit Annual Report
findings.headline: Corporate Health and Safety audit found eight high-priority gaps in risk assessments, accident reporting, and mandatory training monitoring.
findings.detail: The Corporate Health and Safety audit (Limited Assurance) identified weaknesses in completion of high-level risk assessments, reporting and corporate oversight of accidents and incidents, monitoring of mandatory training, and action on non-compliance. Eight high-priority recommendations were made. These gaps expose the council to legal and liability risks.
findings.matters: A lender would be concerned about failures in health and safety compliance and accident reporting, as these represent material liability exposure and potential regulatory non-compliance that could affect financial position.
findings.figures: 8 high-priority recommendations from Corporate Health and Safety audit
findings.quote: Weaknesses were identified in compliance with the completion of high-level risk assessments, the reporting, recording and corporate oversight of accidents and incidents, the monitoring of mandatory training, and the action taken to address areas of non-compliance.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for 2025/26 Internal Audit Annual Report
findings.headline: Four audit reviews resulted in Limited Assurance, indicating significant control and governance weaknesses.
findings.detail: Four areas received Limited Assurance ratings: Electrical Testing (data accuracy, contract management, system data), Markets (insurance gaps, incomplete reconciliations, missing risk assessments), Driver Checks (policy compliance failures, incomplete checks), and Corporate Health and Safety (gaps in risk assessments, accident/incident reporting, mandatory training). Limited Assurance means significant gaps requiring improvement to effectively manage risks.
findings.matters: Multiple significant control gaps across different service areas suggest the council's internal control framework has material weaknesses that could allow risks to materialise unchecked.
findings.figures: 4 audit reviews with Limited Assurance out of 17 total audit reports (24%)
findings.quote: Significant gaps, weaknesses or non-compliance were identified. Improvement is required to the system of governance, risk management and control to effectively manage risks to the achievement of objectives in the area audited

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A Annual Governance Statement and Review of the Code of Corporate Governance
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation decision from Government expected mid-July 2026; council created new Director post to manage transition to new Unitary Authorities
findings.detail: Charnwood faces restructuring into new Unitary Authorities covering Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland, with the Government decision expected mid-July 2026. The council has appointed a Director of Strategy, Transformation and Performance and established steering groups to manage governance arrangements across the affected tier, creating near-term operational and structural change.
findings.matters: Reorganisation is a major structural change creating immediate operational uncertainty, governance complexity, transition costs, and questions about management capacity and financial position during the shadow authority period.
findings.figures: Decision expected mid July 2026
findings.quote: A significant change is Local Government Reorganisation which will require the development of and contribution to governance arrangements for shadow Unitary Authorities and ultimately new Unitary Authorities in Leicester, Leicestershire and Rutland, with the decision from Government expected mid July 2026. To strengthen governance and support delivery of Local Government Reorganisation, the Council has created a new post of Director of Strategy, Transformation and Performance.

findings.paper_title: APPENDIX A Annual Governance Statement and Review of the Code of Corporate Governance
findings.headline: Internal Audit identified areas of limited assurance in Housing, Markets, Driver Checks and Corporate Health and Safety
findings.detail: Four separate audit work areas were rated limited assurance during 2025/26: Housing electrical testing, Markets operations, Driver checks, and Corporate Health and Safety. The council acknowledges implementing 100% of the resulting recommendations, with the audit team monitoring progress. The statement notes this will be updated following finalisation of remaining audit reports.
findings.matters: Limited assurance ratings indicate control gaps in multiple operational areas that could mask financial or service delivery risks affecting the council's operational reliability and credit profile.
findings.figures: Four areas flagged; 100% of recommendations committed to
findings.quote: Internal Audit identified the following areas of limited assurance during the year: Housing - Electrical Testing, Markets, Driver Checks, Corporate Health and Safety. Management have agreed to implement 100% of the resulting recommendations, and implementation will be monitored by the Internal Audit team.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Risk Management (Risk Register)
findings.headline: Housing regulator compliance gap: fire safety actions and electrical testing shortfall self-referred
findings.detail: Charnwood made a self-referral to the Regulator of Social Housing for outstanding fire safety work and a shortfall in the required number of electrical tests on housing stock. Action plans are in place to address the deficiencies. This follows a mock regulatory inspection by HQN.
findings.matters: A regulator self-referral, even with action plans, signals historical non-compliance and carries reputational and operational risk; future regulatory intervention could constrain the council's housing strategy and spending
findings.figures: Specific shortfalls in electrical tests not quantified
findings.quote: Self referral completed in respect of outstanding fire safety actions and a shortfall in the required number of electrical tests completed. Action plans are in place to address these deficiencies.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Risk Management (Risk Register)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation uncertainty is requiring a £500k contingency budget for 2026/27
findings.detail: The council has created an LGR Working Group and commissioned legal advice from neighbouring councils. A Cabinet report in February 2026 will recommend setting aside £500k for capacity (internal and external) to manage LGR engagement while maintaining business as usual. The Government's formal announcement on LGR is expected July 2026.
findings.matters: Organisational restructuring creates strategic planning uncertainty and increases near-term costs; potential merger affects a lender's view of the council's independence and long-term viability
findings.figures: £500k set-aside for LGR capacity; Government announcement due July 2026
findings.quote: There is a recommendation seeking to secure from Cabinet an endorsement to Council for £500k to be set aside for capacity, both internal and external.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Risk Management (Risk Register)
findings.headline: Structural pay reform is being implemented; salary grades and points are being redesigned
findings.detail: Recruitment and retention risk has increased (residual risk 9). The council is proposing changes to pay grades and spinal column points (SCPs), pending Personnel Committee approval in February 2026, for implementation on 1 April 2026. This is a significant structural reform of payroll.
findings.matters: Payroll reform can trigger one-off costs, staff turnover during transition, and forecast volatility; recruitment and retention issues indicate the current pay structure is not competitive
findings.figures: Implementation date 1 April 2026; approval gate February 2026
findings.quote: The Council is proposing to make changes to the pay grades and spinal column points (SCPs) to ensure the pay structure is transparent and fit for the future. If approved at the Personnel Committee February 2026, the proposed changes will be implemented on 1 April 2026.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Risk Management (Risk Register)
findings.headline: HRA Business Plan sustainability is at risk and the council is disposing of sheltered housing to shore up the account
findings.detail: The HRA faces high inherent risk (16) of unmet savings targets leading to a non-viable plan. The council has agreed to dispose of five sheltered accommodation schemes with high void rates and reinvest the proceeds in acquisition. An updated HRA Business Plan is due Q4 2026/27. High void numbers persist and require targeted reduction by Q4 2026/27.
findings.matters: HRA deficits can draw on the general fund or trigger regulatory intervention; disposal of long-term assets to balance a current business plan indicates the plan is not self-sustaining on operations alone
findings.figures: Five sheltered accommodation schemes to be disposed; voids are high but specific numbers not disclosed; Q4 2026/27 for updated plan
findings.quote: Cabinet agreement in place to dispose of five sheltered accommodation schemes containing high numbers of empty properties and reinvest receipts into the acquisition of new accommodation to generate income and support a sustainable HRA financial position.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Risk Management (Risk Register)
findings.headline: Town Hall and Car Parks income has declined, worsening the external funding risk
findings.detail: The council's funding risk (SR3A) has deteriorated specifically because of reduced revenue from the Town Hall and Car Parks. This compounds an already-registered strategic risk around external funding and income generation.
findings.matters: Loss of non-service revenue streams signals either asset underperformance or disposal, affecting the council's ability to maintain reserves or fund services without cuts or borrowing
findings.figures: Not specified; direction of travel noted as deteriorating
findings.quote: Direction of Travel increased due to impact of the revenue from the Town Hall and Car Parks

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management (Q4) Outturn
findings.headline: PWLB rates expected to rise further; market repriced to expect rate hikes in response to inflation shock
findings.detail: On 31 March 2026, the 1-year PWLB Certainty rate was 5.04%; the 5-year, 10-year, 25-year and 50-year rates were 5.28%, 5.72%, 6.29% and 6.08% respectively. The commentary notes that in late February 2026 the yield curve showed expectations of rate cuts, but by late March (following the Middle East conflict) markets were pricing in four rate hikes. The council's own external commentary provider states: 'the Middle East conflict is likely to see inflation spike higher from late spring 2026 through to early 2027.'
findings.matters: Higher PWLB rates increase the council's future debt servicing costs. If the council must borrow to fund the £4.974m HRA unfinanced expenditure and any debt refinancing at these elevated rates (or higher), this will materially impact its revenue budget headroom and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 1-year PWLB 5.04%; 5-year 5.28%; 10-year 5.72%; market pricing in rate hikes as of late March 2026; inflation forecast to breach 4.5% later in 2026
findings.quote: At the start of April 2026, the market expected Bank Rate to increase over the coming months to 4% or 4.25%, from 3.75%, whilst all parts of the curve have also risen substantially through March.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management (Q4) Outturn
findings.headline: Crystallised property fund losses of approximately £1.043m on pooled investments
findings.detail: Two pooled property funds wound up or merged during the year, forcing the council to crystallise capital losses. Federated Hermes Property Unit Trust merged on 15 August 2025; the council was ineligible to transfer to the successor fund and received £2.157m, crystallising a £343k loss on a £2.5m purchase price. Lothbury Property Trust was fully wound up by major investors; the council received £1.8m final distributions against a £2.5m purchase price, crystallising a £700k loss.
findings.matters: These losses reduce the council's usable reserves and are symptoms of the wider pooled fund volatility in the property market post-pandemic. Lenders monitor reserve adequacy closely; these outflows weaken the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: Federated Hermes loss £343k; Lothbury loss £700k; total crystallised losses approximately £1.043m
findings.quote: The Council was ineligible to transfer to the new fund therefore £2.157m was repaid on 20 August 2025, crystallising a capital loss of £343k, between this and the purchase price of £2.5m, which has been fully provided for.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management (Q4) Outturn
findings.headline: Cash-drawdown financing strategy is unsustainable and actively monitored to prevent future cost blow-out
findings.detail: The council explicitly avoided new external borrowing in 2025/26 due to high PWLB rates, instead relying on internal borrowing from cash reserves. While acknowledging this strategy 'has served well over the last few years', the council states it is being 'kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when the Council may not be able to avoid new borrowing.'
findings.matters: This signals the council recognises a cliff edge: once cash reserves are depleted, it will have no choice but to borrow at whatever market rates prevail. If rates remain elevated when that time comes, debt servicing costs will spike. The council's own concern about timing is material to credit risk.
findings.figures: Internal investments held £16.21m on 31 March 2026 (down from £37.35m a year prior); average investment balance £37m
findings.quote: The policy of avoiding new borrowing by running down spare cash balances has served well over the last few years. However, this was kept under review to avoid incurring higher borrowing costs in the future when the Council may not be able to avoid new borrowing to finance capital expenditure and/or the refinancing of maturing debt.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management (Q4) Outturn
findings.headline: HRA unfinanced capital expenditure of £4,974m will require external borrowing when cash reserves deplete
findings.detail: The HRA financed only £11,473m of £16,447m capital expenditure in 2025/26, leaving £4,974m unfinanced. The council funded this gap through internal borrowing (cash drawdown) rather than PWLB borrowing to avoid elevated costs. The council explicitly states future borrowing will be necessary: 'the need to borrow long-term to fund net unfinanced capital expenditure and naturally maturing debt will be necessary.'
findings.matters: Lenders need to know when the council will access external markets and at what rates. PWLB 1-year rates stood at 5.04% on 31 March 2026, with the council's own commentary expecting them to rise further due to inflation. This shapes the council's future debt servicing costs and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: HRA unfinanced capital expenditure £4,974m; 1-year PWLB Certainty rate 5.04% (31/03/26); 5-year rate 5.28%
findings.quote: Going forward, the need to borrow long-term to fund net unfinanced capital expenditure and naturally maturing debt will be necessary. An update to the Capital Plan is scheduled for the autumn which will include a section on future financing options and proposals.

findings.paper_title: ANNEX Cnl 23 Feb 2026 Item 06.1 2026-27 GF and HRA Revenue Budgets and Council Tax (Cab Report)
findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation costs and existential uncertainty; council to be subsumed into unitary by 31 March 2028
findings.detail: The budget creates a new Local Government Reorganisation (LGR) Reserve with £500k allocated for 2026/27, to be funded from the Business Rate Pool Reserve. The paper notes potential costs will 'likely include redundancy costs relating to senior staff, additional staffing required for data collection and management of transition projects.' The council's s151 officer describes LGR as creating 'an existential level of uncertainty for the Council' with all Shire District councils expected to cease by 31 March 2028.
findings.matters: LGR creates profound uncertainty about the council's future and finances. Redundancy costs and transition spending will consume reserves. The statutory bodies merging may have different financial positions and governance, affecting debt servicing and covenant compliance.
findings.figures: LGR Reserve created 2026/27: £500k; LGR Reserve projected balance 31 March 2027: £500k
findings.quote: the potential costs of LGR transition which are likely to include redundancy costs relating to senior staff, additional staffing required for data collection and management of transition projects

findings.paper_title: ANNEX Cnl 23 Feb 2026 Item 06.1 2026-27 GF and HRA Revenue Budgets and Council Tax (Cab Report)
findings.headline: Business Rates Pool discontinued; council using £1.902m NNDR Rebasing Reserve to cover baseline reset
findings.detail: Following the Fair Funding Review, the Leicestershire Business Rates Pool is being discontinued from 31 March 2026 after historically generating significant returns for the council. The 2026/27 budget relies on a £1.902m drawdown from the NNDR Rebasing Reserve created for this transition, with further drawdowns forecast for 2027/28 (£1.976m) and 2028/29 (£877k). By 2028/29, the rebasing reserve will be exhausted.
findings.matters: Loss of business rates pool income and reliance on one-time reserve to manage the baseline reset represents permanent loss of a revenue source. This increases the council's funding dependency and reduces flexibility.
findings.figures: 2026/27 NNDR Rebasing Reserve drawdown: £1.902m; 2027/28: £1.976m; 2028/29: £877m; NNDR Rebasing Reserve projected balance: £2.853k (31 March 2027)
findings.quote: new rules for the calculation of retained business rates combined with baseline 'rebasing' has led the Leicestershire Treasurers group to conclude the Pool should be discontinued from 31 March 2026

findings.paper_title: ANNEX Cnl 23 Feb 2026 Item 06.1 2026-27 GF and HRA Revenue Budgets and Council Tax (Cab Report)
findings.headline: Disrepair and damp & mould claims creating £595k legal and remedial cost pressure in HRA
findings.detail: The HRA budget shows £350k for legal costs related to disrepair claims and £245k for responsive repairs to address disrepair and damp & mould issues. The paper notes ongoing compliance pressures around the implementation of Awaab's Law (dealing with mould and condensation). These are emerging liabilities being driven by regulatory compliance requirements and tenant claims.
findings.matters: Growing disrepair and damp & mould claims indicate both regulatory compliance risks (Awaab's Law obligations) and contingent liabilities. Legal costs for disrepair claims suggest the council is exposed to tenant claims that could grow, and the conditions triggering these claims are ongoing.
findings.figures: Legal costs for disrepair claims: £350k; responsive repairs for disrepair and damp & mould: £245k
findings.quote: The key risk in respect of the repairs and maintenance budget is the potential increase in activity arising from the review of the decent home's standard, the application of Awaab's law and the volume of necessary unreported works arising from the stock condition survey.

findings.paper_title: ANNEX Cnl 23 Feb 2026 Item 06.1 2026-27 GF and HRA Revenue Budgets and Council Tax (Cab Report)
findings.headline: Void property repairs crisis: £2.046m budget pressure from 376 voids requiring high-cost relet repairs
findings.detail: The council repaired 376 void properties by end of October 2025, significantly above normal levels, resulting in a £2.046m budget increase for void repairs in 2026/27. The paper notes 'The backlog on these voids are forecast to be reduced to normal levels in the autumn of 2026.' This represents a substantial operational and cost pressure affecting housing stock turnover and income collection.
findings.matters: Large void backlogs indicate service delivery problems and revenue loss from empty properties. High repair costs reduce the financial returns from the housing stock and strain cash flow during the period of remediation.
findings.figures: Void repairs budget increase 2026/27: £2.046m; void loss budgeted at 5% (approximately £1.3m) of rent income
findings.quote: The amounts required to repair void properties and relet them faster have increased significantly in 2025/26 with 376 voids repaired to the end of October 2025. This has led to an increase in the budget for 2026/27 of £2.046m

findings.paper_title: ANNEX Cnl 23 Feb 2026 Item 06.1 2026-27 GF and HRA Revenue Budgets and Council Tax (Cab Report)
findings.headline: HRA deficit growing despite 4.80% rent increase; financing reserve depleted to £116k by March 2027
findings.detail: The HRA shows a deficit of £2.165m in 2026/27, up £1.463m from the £701k deficit in 2025/26. Despite increasing dwelling rents by 4.80% in line with MHCLG guidance, the council cannot balance housing finances. The HRA Financing Reserve, which stood at £17.52m in 2024/25, is projected to fall to just £116k by end of March 2027. The council explicitly states the reserve 'can no longer be used to repay debt or finance capital expenditure' and loan repayment and capital spending 'will have to be financed by increased borrowing'.
findings.matters: HRA reserve collapse indicates the housing account is in financial stress. Depletion of reserves that previously financed capital work forces debt increases, materially worsening the council's financial position and borrowing profile.
findings.figures: HRA deficit 2026/27: £2.165m (vs £701k in 2025/26); HRA Financing Reserve: £17.524m (2024/25 actual) → £116k (2026/27 projected)
findings.quote: due to the £3.93m deficit in 2024/25 and the forecast outturn deficit for 2025/26 of £2.5m the reserve can no longer be used to repay debt or finance capital expenditure. Instead, the loan repayment and the capital expenditure will have to be financed by increased borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 3 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Authorised borrowing limits have been raised to reflect projected increase in HRA external borrowing.
findings.detail: The Authorised Limit for External Debt has been increased: General Fund from £0 to £20m; HRA from £78.2m to £130m (2026/27) and £150m (2027/28). This is explicit acknowledgement that HRA borrowing is about to rise materially. The paper notes limits 'show an increase from previous years reflecting the projected increase in HRA borrowing.'
findings.matters: Raising debt ceilings is a leading indicator of anticipated borrowing need. It signals council officers expect to be back to council for approval to borrow at higher levels within months.
findings.figures: Authorised Limit HRA 2026/27 £130m (previously £78.2m); 2027/28 £150m.
findings.quote: It should be noted that the authorised limits (as shown in the table below) has been set based on the current capital expenditure and funding plans within the Capital Strategy. Limits show an increase from previous years reflecting the projected increase in HRA borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 3 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Subsidy buyout loans taken in 2005 are now maturing and must be refinanced or repaid, with no complete 30-year business plan yet in place.
findings.detail: The council borrowed to exit the Housing Subsidy regime (government-imposed). These loans are maturing: £1m repaid October 2024, £2m October 2025. The repayment schedule extends to 2061. Repayment or refinancing decisions 'will be considered alongside the next iteration of the HRA Business Plan' — implying the plan is not yet complete. The council notes 'The HRA data set is currently limited, however a 30 year business plan is being developed.'
findings.matters: Forced refinancing at current rates (PWLB 10-year at 5.39% as at 22 Dec 2025) exposes the council to rate risk. Absence of a completed long-term HRA business plan means the council cannot yet demonstrate the affordability of housing commitments or have full visibility of future borrowing needs.
findings.figures: £1m repaid October 2024; £2m repaid October 2025; twenty-four loans repayable between 2024 and 2061; total HRA external debt £78.19m.
findings.quote: Existing loans taken out to finance buy-out of the Housing Subsidy arrangements (a process imposed by government) are now maturing such that they must be repaid or refinanced. Their maturity dates will be considered alongside the next iteration of the HRA Business Plan.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 3 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA financing fund will be depleted by end of 2025/26, forcing material external borrowing for housing capital and debt repayment.
findings.detail: The HRA Financing Fund—a reserve used annually for capital expenditure and loan repayments—will be completely exhausted in 2025/26. From 2026/27 onwards, the council cannot fund its housing capital programme from retained cash and must borrow externally. HRA total CFR is projected to rise from £86.3m (2025/26 forecast) to £100.3m (2026/27) to £114.3m (2027/28), with external debt following.
findings.matters: A reserve-funded council losing that reserve source signals financial tightening and forces it into bond markets at prevailing rates, increasing debt-service costs. The HRA is typically a council's largest debt portfolio; forecasted external borrowing now rises from £76.8m to £100.8m over two years.
findings.figures: HRA Financing Fund depletes to zero in 2025/26; HRA external debt £78.2m (March 2025) → £76.8m (2025/26 forecast) → £88.8m (2027/28) → £100.8m (2028/29). HRA CFR £86.3m → £100.3m → £114.3m.
findings.quote: Projections show the depletion of the HRA financing fund in 2025/26 (a reserve previously available for funding capital expenditure and loan repayments) leading to an 'underborrowed' position. To maintain capital expenditure a significant level of external borrowing will be required.

findings.paper_title: Background Paper - General Fund Budget Analysis
findings.headline: Council budget depends on achieving £2.4m of managed savings
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget includes £2,393k of Managed Savings that must be delivered for the budget to balance. These are broken down as £1,885k from employee cost reductions, £438k from supplies and services cuts, partially offset by £69k additional building costs and £140k income generation. This represents approximately 9.5% of the council's total net expenditure.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether planned savings are realistic and committed. If the council fails to deliver these reductions, it will either overspend or face a funding shortfall. The scale suggests budget pressures are material.
findings.figures: Managed Savings: £2,393k; Employee reductions: £1,885k; Supplies reductions: £438k; Total net expenditure: £25,071k

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Income stream portfolio variance of ±£0.5m across fees and charges; leisure sector contracting at break-even only
findings.detail: Council income of ~£13m annually from fees and charges faces multiple headwinds. Planning fees are cyclical with ±£0.25m variance. Post-COVID, leisure sector income targets break-even only (no profit). Markets income remains depressed. Town Hall and car parking showing some recovery but uncertain. Portfolio-level variance estimated at ±£0.5m, representing 3-4% of budgeted income.
findings.matters: A £0.5m adverse income variance would consume working balance more quickly than projected. Lenders should note that income recovery assumptions are cautious but leisure income specifically contributes nothing to reserves.
findings.figures: Total annual income ~£13m; planning fee variance ±£0.25m; portfolio variance ±£0.5m; leisure at break-even
findings.quote: Leisure centres – post the COVID pandemic, the entire leisure sector has come under increasing pressure. The central case is that the leisure contract (and any new contract) will enable provision of leisure services at break-even (nil cost, nil revenue)... Considered in total as a portfolio, income may realistically be plus or minus £0.5m versus the budgeted figures.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Structural Change Order imminent, likely to restrict council acquisitions, disposals, pay/grading, and reserve use
findings.detail: Government is expected to issue a Structural Change Order (SCO) in the coming months restricting council activity ahead of LGR. This device 'may cover areas such as asset acquisitions and disposals, pay and grading, and reserve levels' and 'may replace or supersede pre-existing Council strategies and policies of all types.'
findings.matters: An SCO would override council plans and constrain financial management flexibility during the LGR transition period. This reduces the council's ability to respond to emerging financial pressures and could affect how reserves are used.
findings.figures: Timing: expected 'coming months' from January 2026 writing; applies through to 1 April 2028
findings.quote: A final point to raise is the likely imposition of a 'Structural Change Order' (SCO) in the coming months. This device, used in previous unitarisation arrangements, places restrictions on legacy councils in the period prior to the new authority coming into effect, and may cover areas such as asset acquisitions and disposals, pay and grading, and reserve levels. Clearly, the Council will wish to comply with the Order if and when this comes into effect, and in practice the SCO may replace or supersede pre-existing Council strategies and policies of all types.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Agency staffing costs of £1.2m net remain unresolved; pay award risk of £500k upside in each year
findings.detail: The council budgets £2.4m for agency staff offset by £1.2m permanent salary savings (net £100k/month). Recruitment and retention initiatives are underway but 'unlikely to provide a complete panacea'. Pay awards are assumed at 3.5% for 2026/27-2027/28, but if awards exceed assumptions, downside risk is estimated at £500k per year (each 1% variance on £20m payroll = £200k).
findings.matters: Agency costs are non-negotiable and persistent; they constrain available budget for other pressures. With £20m payroll budget, pay award variance is material. Lenders need to assess whether these costs are stabilising or structural.
findings.figures: £2.4m agency budget; £1.2m salary savings offset; net £1.2m (£100k/month); pay award risk £500k per year
findings.quote: Maintaining the Council's service delivery standards has required use of agency staff for certain difficult-to-recruit key roles... it is unlikely that these will provide a complete panacea

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Commercial property investment strategy ended; borrowing restrictions prevent further acquisitions
findings.detail: The £22m commercial property portfolio (generating ~£1.6m rental income) can no longer be expanded. Changes to the Prudential Code 'will effectively prevent the Council acquiring commercial property using debt'. Additionally, 2026/27 rental income drops to £1.3m due to an agreed rent-free period with one tenant (£300k reduction).
findings.matters: The council's capital strategy has shifted from growth to stasis. This removes a revenue-generating strategy and constrains the council's financial flexibility. The specific £300k rental reduction is a near-term income hit.
findings.figures: Portfolio cost £22m; current annual rental ~£1.6m; 2026/27 rental £1.3m (£300k reduction); no further acquisitions planned
findings.quote: The Council has built up a portfolio of commercial properties for investment purposes at a cost of £22m, generating gross annual rental returns of around £1.6m... the Council's ability to make additional commercial property acquisitions is now very restricted due to reduced access to Public Works Loan Board borrowing, and changes to the 'Prudential Code' which will effectively prevent the Council acquiring commercial property using debt.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) income uncertainty of £700k between government assessment and council's internal review
findings.detail: Government indicates £3.1m EPR income for 2026/27, but the council's internal review concludes this is overstated due to incorrect waste tonnage figures used by DeFRA and budgets £2.4m instead. Pessimistic case shows further potential reduction of up to £500k if producers reduce packaging.
findings.matters: This £700k variance affects net service expenditure and could reduce available reserves. If actual EPR proves closer to government figures, the council's position improves; if pessimistic scenario occurs, working balance absorbs the cost.
findings.figures: Government estimate £3.1m; council budget £2.4m; pessimistic case £0-500k reduction
findings.quote: The government have informed us that EPR income for 2025/26 and 2026/27 will be around £3.1m but internal review suggests this is overstated due to incorrect waste tonnage figures being used by DeFRA. Internal calculations suggest that the correct figure should be around £2.4m

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account facing significant cost pressures from regulation and construction inflation
findings.detail: The HRA is under strain from rent capping limits (CPI-linked), Awaab's Law regulatory costs, and rising construction costs. The council is developing a new 30-year business plan and pursuing rent equalisation and service charge rebalancing, but maintaining the minimum £1.5m reserve (£200 per house plus £0.5m) is a stated challenge through LGR transition.
findings.matters: HRA pressure could require General Fund support or force service reductions; housing is a core council service. Lenders need to assess whether the General Fund working balance might be drawn down to support housing.
findings.figures: HRA reserve minimum £1.5m (£200 per house + £0.5m block sum); rent capped at CPI for several years
findings.quote: In contrast to the General Fund, the Housing Revenue Account (HRA) is experiencing significant cost pressures. The impact of regulations constraining rent increases over several years combined with rising construction costs and increasing regulatory burdens in the housing sector, such as Awaab's Law has created a challenging environment in which to manage and maintain our housing stock.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account identified as 'most challenging financial area' facing sustained pressure from rent controls, cost inflation, and regulatory burden
findings.detail: The Council's HRA is under pressure from restricted rent increases (inability to raise rents as needed), cost increases above general inflation, and increased regulatory burden from the Environment Act 2021. The CFO states that minimum reserve balances will be maintained for 2026/27 with active work underway to maintain this position in future years, indicating recognition of this as a sustained structural challenge.
findings.matters: HRA deficits could eventually require subsidy from the general fund, weakening overall financial position. The active reserve management suggests the council recognizes the risk that cost pressures could outpace restricted rent income.
findings.figures: Minimum reserve for HRA set at £200 per house plus £0.5m
findings.quote: The most challenging financial area for the Council is that of the Housing Revenue Account (HRA). In common with the national position for Councils that maintain their own social housing stock, a combination of restricted rent increases, cost increases above the general rate of inflation and an increased regulatory burden has put significant pressure on HRA finances.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 7 Section 25 Report
findings.headline: All Shire District councils due to cease by 31 March 2028 under Government Local Government Reorganisation proposal
findings.detail: The Council faces existential uncertainty due to the proposed cessation of Shire District councils by 31 March 2028, announced in the Government White Paper on Devolution and Local Government Reorganisation (December 2024). The CFO notes that reserves are adequate over this timeframe, and funding certainty extends to 2028/29, but the council's structural dissolution creates fundamental uncertainty.
findings.matters: Any lending to this council must account for the fact that it will cease to exist in its current form by March 2028, affecting loan tenor, repayment assumptions, and the council's post-2028 obligations.
findings.figures: 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The biggest implication of this paper is the proposed cessation of all Shire District councils by 31 March 2028. This creates an existential level of uncertainty for the Council, but paradoxically, it can be stated with relative certainty that the Council's reserves are adequate over this timeframe.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Treasury investment returns critical to 2026/27 budget; council betting on continued high interest rate environment
findings.detail: The council describes investment returns from its cash holdings as forming 'a vital component' of the 2026/27 budget. Base rates are currently 3.75% (January 2026) and forecast to fall to 2.75% by December 2026. The council's strategy assumes it will lock in longer-term investments (6-24 months) at current rates before yields decline.
findings.matters: Budget sustainability depends on treasury returns. If interest rates fall faster than forecasted or the council's cash position deteriorates, this income stream shrinks materially. The HRA reserve depletion already signals tightening liquidity.
findings.figures: Base rate January 2026: 3.75%; forecast December 2026: 2.75%; forecast December 2027: 2%; investment strategy assumes locking in 6-24 month maturities
findings.quote: Finally, it is again true to say that the anticipated investment returns derived from the Council's significant cash balances form a key component of the (proposed) 2026/27 budget.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: All capital planning decisions constrained by Local Government Reorganisation deadline of 31 March 2028; only schemes deliverable within 21 months will be initiated
findings.detail: The council is merging into a new unitary authority by April 2028. The Capital Plan was redrawn to cover only 1 October 2025 to 31 March 2028. A £5m allocation for economic regeneration was deleted because schemes cannot be delivered within the remaining life of the council. Focus is now on 'business as usual' asset refreshment only.
findings.matters: The LGR deadline creates an artificial constraint on the council's ability to undertake longer-term capital investment. This reduces strategic flexibility and means the council may not be able to complete planned infrastructure projects. A Strategic Change Order from government will likely impose further restrictions.
findings.figures: £5m regeneration allocation deleted; capital plan horizon compressed from traditional 3 years to 30 months (to March 2028); unitary merger date April 1, 2028
findings.quote: This Capital Strategy is focussed on the 2026/27 financial year, but all plans and decision making are coloured by the run-in to LGR. In practice this means a focus on ensuring that 'business as usual' services continue to be delivered to a high standard and that capital projects are unlikely to be initiated unless they can be delivered within the remaining life of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: Large HRA debt portfolio from 2012 Self-Financing now entering repayment maturity schedule
findings.detail: The council took on £79.2m in PWLB loans in 2012 to purchase its housing stock. The first tranches have now matured: £1m repaid October 2024, £2m October 2025. Repayments continue annually, ramping to £5m annually from 2042-57. The council refinanced the October 2025 repayment internally rather than from external sources, indicating cash pressure.
findings.matters: The maturity profile shows the HRA is already committed to substantial ongoing repayments for the next 37 years, creating a structural constraint on HRA liquidity and flexibility. Internal financing of repayments suggests available cash is tightening.
findings.figures: Original loan £79.2m; first repayment £1m October 2024; second repayment £2m October 2025; future annual repayments rise to £5m annually 2042-2057; total repaid by 2062
findings.quote: The loan maturing in 2024 a was repaid using the HRA Financing Fund. Due to cost pressure and use of reserves within the HRA in recent months it has been considered prudent to effectively refinance the loan repaid in October 2025 via internal borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: IFRS9 override protection expires; commercial property portfolio fair value losses now impact council accounts
findings.detail: The council holds £22.5m in commercial property investments (car showroom, offices, industrial units). An override allowing councils to defer recognising fair value losses expired 31 March 2025. Going forward, any impairment in the portfolio's value will directly impact the general fund and potentially the council's budget-setting ability. The council says it will mitigate by diverting rental receipts to create a loss provision.
findings.matters: The portfolio is now exposed to direct accounting impact from property market downturns, and the mitigation (diverting rental income) reduces usable cash. A material property downturn could force recognition of losses.
findings.figures: Commercial property portfolio £22.5m; 2026/27 expected rental income £1.1m net; Property Reserve anticipated at £1.25m by 31 March 2026; £0.1m per annum allocated annually to reserve
findings.quote: However, the override is (currently) time limited to 31 March 2025 and a major downturn in the value of specific assets, or the property market generally, represents a clear risk in future financial periods

findings.paper_title: Enc. 2 for MTFO 26-29 + Capital Strategy, Treasury Management Strategy Statement, Minimum Revenue Provision Policy and Annual Investment Strategy 2026-27
findings.headline: HRA Financing Fund depleted; additional borrowing needed sooner than planned, potentially from 2026
findings.detail: The document states that cost pressures and reserve use have shortened the timeline for HRA borrowing. The council previously expected to avoid new HRA borrowing for longer, but rising costs in landlord services mean it may now be needed within the current financial year or next. The council has already refinanced the October 2025 loan repayment through internal borrowing rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: Deteriorating HRA liquidity and forced earlier-than-planned external borrowing signals cash flow stress in the housing operation, which accounts for £79.2m of the council's debt.
findings.figures: £79.2m original HRA borrowing portfolio; repayments began October 2024 and October 2025; additional borrowing potentially required from 2026
findings.quote: A combination of investment in landlord services and rising costs have resulted in depletion of the Financing Fund such that the date where HRA additional borrowing required is likely to be sooner than previously anticipated, potentially from 2026.

findings.paper_title: Background Papers Combined BSR Audit June 2025 (Item 10 Building Control)
findings.headline: Regulatory enforcement action threatened if remediation not complete by 22 September 2025
findings.detail: The Health and Safety Executive has set a 22 September 2025 deadline for the council to provide evidence of remediation. Failure to respond will result in escalating enforcement: first an Improvement Notice, potentially followed by a Serious Contravention Notice under Building Act 1984.
findings.matters: This creates explicit regulatory enforcement risk within three months; failure brings statutory notices and potential service restrictions
findings.figures: 22 September 2025
findings.quote: If you do not respond demonstrating acceptable action has been taken by the deadline, BSR may take further enforcement measures, which may include the service of an Improvement Notice under Section 58Z4, or a Serious Contravention Notice under Section 58Z5 of the Building Act 1984 (as amended by Building Safety Act 2022).

findings.paper_title: Background Papers Combined BSR Audit June 2025 (Item 10 Building Control)
findings.headline: Multiple building control projects abandoned or without defined next steps
findings.detail: Sample testing found four projects inadequately reviewed: a loft conversion with no action for 11 months; an office extension with last contact in March 2024; a retail conversion marked complete with no inspection records; and a school project untouched since July 2022. None have defined next steps.
findings.matters: Abandoned project oversight indicates systemic operational failure; it creates compliance and safety gaps in statutory building control and signals process breakdown
findings.figures: Four projects identified: BN/24/1013/1, RA/24/0148/1, FP/24/0782/1, FP/22/1093/1
findings.quote: Sample testing identified that the following projects had not been reviewed appropriately. BN/24/1013/1-Loft conversion- in flight - no actions since 19/9/24- next steps not defined. RA/24/0148/1 -Increase office space- in flight - last contact was 13/3/24 – next steps not defined. FP/24/0782/1- Retail conversion -completed- no inspection information provided. FP/22/1093/1- School- in flight -no actions since 11/7/22- next steps not defined.

findings.paper_title: Background Papers Combined BSR Audit June 2025 (Item 10 Building Control)
findings.headline: No formal performance evaluation of building control function in 2024/25
findings.detail: The council failed to conduct the mandatory annual formal evaluation of its building control function during 2024/25. While a yearly LABC audit is planned for 2025/26 to maintain ISO 9001 registration, the internal audit review has not been scheduled.
findings.matters: Absence of formal evaluation is itself a contravention and suggests lack of internal control and monitoring; it leaves performance gaps undetected
findings.figures: Financial year 2024/25
findings.quote: There was no formal evaluation of the performance and effectiveness of the building control functions in financial year 2024/25. The 2025/26 internal audit plan is currently under development but a review of the building control function has not been determined.

findings.paper_title: Background Papers Combined BSR Audit June 2025 (Item 10 Building Control)
findings.headline: Building Control Manager operating outside their legal registration
findings.detail: The manager holding a Class 1 Registered Building Inspector registration is undertaking restricted functions and activities beyond that registration level. This is a direct breach of competence requirements under Building Act 1984.
findings.matters: This is a regulatory breach that creates liability and enforcement risk; it indicates governance failure at the leadership level of a statutory function
findings.figures: Class 1 RBI
findings.quote: The Building Control Manager is a registered Class 1 RBI undertaking restricted functions and activities outside of their competence and registration level.

findings.paper_title: Background Papers Combined BSR Audit June 2025 (Item 10 Building Control)
findings.headline: Building control function is inadequately resourced
findings.detail: The inspection found the council's building control is under-staffed and cannot discharge its statutory duties effectively. The council acknowledges this as a known issue and has planned recruitment for 1 Principal BC Surveyor, 2 Registered Building Inspectors, and 1 Trainee Surveyor, but recruitment remains incomplete.
findings.matters: Under-resourced building control creates regulatory risk and enforcement action risk; it also signals broader capacity constraints in the council
findings.figures: 1 x Principal BC Surveyor, 2 x RBI, 1 x Trainee Surveyor planned
findings.quote: Charnwood Borough Council building control function is inadequately resourced to discharge its building control restricted functions and activities appropriately and effectively. This is a known issue reflected in the councils resource plan (set out in the Internal Organisational Chart 10/12/24).

findings.paper_title: AC 18 Nov 2025 CBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: No disaster recovery or business continuity plan for finance system Unit 4, rated AMBER
findings.detail: The council has no disaster recovery or business continuity plan if Unit 4 (the SaaS finance system) becomes unavailable. The auditor rated this AMBER and identified increased risk of data loss and delayed recovery. Management's response relies on the SaaS contract rather than establishing its own resilience.
findings.matters: Absence of finance system continuity planning creates operational risk. For a lender assessing council resilience, inability to maintain financial reporting and cash management in adverse scenarios is a material concern.
findings.figures: AMBER rating (significant effect on financial statements)
findings.quote: The Council does not have a disaster recovery plan or business continuity plan in place in the event of Unit 4 services being unavailable. Risk- There is an increased likelihood of data loss and/or delays in data recovery due to weaknesses in the backup and recovery processes.

findings.paper_title: AC 18 Nov 2025 CBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Asset revaluation de-minimis threshold of £10k systematically excludes £210k of revaluation gains from accounts
findings.detail: The council applies a £10k threshold for asset valuation movements, resulting in £210k of upwards revaluations not being recorded in the fixed asset register or accounts for 2024/25. This systematic understatement of asset values was identified as an unadjusted misstatement.
findings.matters: Systematic non-recording of asset revaluations misrepresents the council's balance sheet and asset base. This practice distorts financial position and limits comparability year to year.
findings.figures: £210k of upwards valuation movements excluded; de-minimis threshold £10k; asset valuations in accounts £453,113k
findings.quote: Management applies a £10k threshold for applying valuation movements identified by the valuer to assets include din the fixed asset register and subsequently the accounts. As a result, for 2024/25 £210k of upwards valuation movements have not been reflected in the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: AC 18 Nov 2025 CBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Capital expenditure of £566k relating to 2024/25 was not accrued as creditors at year end
findings.detail: The audit identified capital expenditure payments made post 31 March 2025 that related to 2024/25 but had not been accrued in the financial statements. This AMBER-rated issue was left unadjusted. Management attributed it to isolated incidents related to two specific officers.
findings.matters: Failure to accrue year-end liabilities understates creditors and masks cash position. This indicates weak controls over the cut-off of transactions, a core accounting control.
findings.figures: £566k unadjusted misstatement
findings.quote: We identified a number of capital expenditure payments made post 31 March 2025 that related to the 2024/25 financial year but had not been accrued for in the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: AC 18 Nov 2025 CBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: No journal approval process in place, rated AMBER, creating fraud and error risk
findings.detail: The audit found no approval process for journals before posting. Management rejected the auditor's recommendation for an approval process, relying instead on reconciliation reviews for key accounts and staff training. This is an AMBER-rated control weakness affecting the most basic financial accounting control.
findings.matters: Absence of journal controls is a fundamental fraud risk and undermines confidence in reported numbers. It is exactly the type of control weakness that creates material misstatement opportunity.
findings.figures: AMBER rating (significant effect on financial statements)
findings.quote: No approval process is in place for journals which could lead to incorrect or fraudulent journal being posted.

findings.paper_title: AC 18 Nov 2025 CBC Audit Findings Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Council failed to comply with Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015 by not publishing Annual Governance Statement with draft accounts
findings.detail: On 01 July 2025, Charnwood published draft financial statements without the required Annual Governance Statement. The council re-published both on 29 September 2025 and restarted the public inspection period to 07 November 2025. This is a breach of section 15 of the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015.
findings.matters: Regulatory non-compliance in financial reporting deadlines signals governance control failures that lenders use to assess the reliability of the finance function.
findings.figures: Initial publication 01 July 2025; Re-publication 29 September 2025; Restarted inspection period 07 November 2025
findings.quote: the authority may not have fully complied with the requirements of the Accounts and Audit Regulations 2015 in relation to the commencement of the period for the exercise of public rights on initial publication.

news_drafts.headline: £17.9m of capital budgets from 2025-26 did not progress and have been rolled into 2026-27
news_drafts.lead: A lender would need to assess whether the council has sufficient delivery capacity and resources to execute an enlarged capital programme without further slippage. Sustained capital delays can indicate resource constraints, project management weaknesses,…

news_drafts.headline: Officers and Scrutiny Committee hold opposing views on whether to spend down reserves before unitarisation
news_drafts.lead: This unresolved policy disagreement affects the financial position the new unitary authority will inherit and signals governance tension over reserve management during a critical transition

news_drafts.headline: Structural Changes Order from March 2027 creates a narrow window to deploy reserves before local government reorganisation takes effect
news_drafts.lead: The impending restriction order creates both time pressure to deploy reserves and regulatory risk if spending decisions are made incorrectly; the new unitary council will inherit the consequences of deployment decisions made now
